text:
Ethan Park: dropping here for arch review async. main question: where should gate evaluation live for Dedicated staged rollouts? options we’ve floated:
1) policy engine does metric queries + gate evaluation inline
2) separate gate-evaluator service/job evaluates over windows + writes results/state, policy engine only enforces current stage weight + blocks on HOLD

concerns: failure modes + “metrics lie” (stale/missing/biased metrics causing us to advance when we shouldn’t or hold forever). would love routing + SRE + security takes.

Jordan Lee: strong -1 to putting metric queries inside policy engine. policy engine is on hot path + should stay deterministic and low-latency. also: if prom/query backend flakes, routing decisions become nondeterministic.

Mina Haddad: +1. routing needs a stable “current allocation plan” snapshot. if the evaluator is querying metrics at request time, you’ll get different answers per request / per region. nightmare to debug.

Logan Wright: also metric query cost/cardinality. doing queries per decision is going to be unbounded. we already see query fanout issues when people slap per-model/per-tenant labels.

Sean Gallagher: from oncall perspective: if gate eval is embedded in policy engine, failures look like “routing is broken”. we want clean separation: routing enforces last-known-good state; evaluator is the thing that can degrade/lag.

Allison Grant: +1 separation. also makes dashboards clearer: “evaluator lagging” vs “routing applying stage weights incorrectly”.

Benji Okafor: control plane angle: separate evaluator lets us persist evaluations as events with reasons. we can store `gate_result` + `metrics_freshness` + `sample_size` etc. if policy engine is doing it, we lose auditability unless we log everything (and we *won’t*).

Marcus Lin: audit + compliance: approvals and automatic holds/rollbacks need structured events. if the decision is “implicit in policy engine behavior” it becomes hard to prove who/what/when. separate evaluator with explicit state transitions is much easier to defend.

Keiko Yamamoto: infra/guardrails: also need to gate on capacity headroom signals (gpu util, queue depth). those signals can be delayed under incident conditions. evaluator should treat missing/freshness issues as HOLD (fail safe), not “keep going”.

Ethan Park: ok seems consensus leaning #2. can we enumerate failure modes + how we want to behave?

Sean Gallagher: failure modes list (first pass):
- metrics backend latency spikes (queries return late)
- metrics gaps (missing scrapes / exporter down)
- partial ingestion (one region/pool missing series)
- evaluator lag (job behind schedule)
- bad thresholds (too strict -> stuck; too loose -> advance into incident)
- “metrics lie”: wrong aggregation / sampling bias; e.g. p95 looks fine but tail is melting; or queue depth averaged hides spikes

Logan Wright: + “cardinality explosion” where query silently drops series (or times out) and you end up evaluating on partial data without realizing it.

Thomas Baird: yup. we’ve seen people query `histogram_quantile` over a subset b/c label join fails and it returns something that looks plausible.

Mina Haddad: for “metrics lie” re tail: we should be careful about what p95 means w batching + queueing. if queue depth rises, service time might look ok but end-to-end latency is bad.

Jordan Lee: policy engine integration idea:
- evaluator produces a signed-ish (or at least versioned) `StageEvaluation` record in control plane
- routing reads `rollout_state` (stage + status) from control plane cache
- only transitions stage when status is `APPROVED` and all required gates are `PASS`
- if evaluator status unknown/STALE => `HOLD`

Ethan Park: what constitutes STALE? i keep hearing “metrics freshness check” but want something crisp.

Allison Grant: propose evaluator emits `observed_window_end_ts` + `query_ts` + `data_delay_seconds`. SLO: we only trust results if `data_delay_seconds <= X` and `window_coverage >= Y%`.

Logan Wright: we can measure query-time “max sample timestamp” per series depending on backend. simplest: store `latest_datapoint_ts` for each gate query result (if backend returns it). if not, we approximate by scraping timestamp. either way, evaluator can enforce: `now - latest_datapoint_ts <= freshness_budget`.

Thomas Baird: and require minimum sample size. e.g. for error rate: at least N requests in window OR else treat as INCONCLUSIVE and HOLD. otherwise 1 request can make error rate 0% and pass.

Sean Gallagher: +1. and for latency histograms: require enough observations (sum of buckets) before trusting quantile.

Mina Haddad: question: do we want “HOLD until manual approve” vs “auto rollback” on gate failure?

Sean Gallagher: for Dedicated, default should be HOLD on *inconclusive* (missing/stale) and HOLD on *fail* for beta, with optional auto-rollback if gate fails hard and we have a known-good previous config. SRE wants human in loop at least initially.

Jordan Lee: agree. auto rollback is risky if failure is caused by evaluator/metrics. you don’t want to churn the pool.

Ethan Park: so rule-of-thumb:
- gate FAIL w fresh+enough data => hold (and maybe rollback if policy says)
- gate INCONCLUSIVE (missing/stale/low-sample) => hold, no rollback
- evaluator unhealthy => hold all rollouts, prevent stage advancement

Marcus Lin: + emit audit event on HOLD reason. compliance folks will ask “why did system stop?” and “who resumed?”

Benji Okafor: data model wise, I’m thinking each gate evaluation writes something like:
```
result: PASS|FAIL|INCONCLUSIVE
reason_code: LATENCY_P95_EXCEEDED|METRICS_STALE|INSUFFICIENT_SAMPLES|QUERY_ERROR|...
window_start, window_end
query_executed_at
observations_count
value_summary: "p95=842ms threshold=700ms" (string)
```
(not nested; but we can store as text fields)

Allison Grant: also need to be explicit about evaluation interval. if gates are 5m windows but evaluator runs every 30s, we should not “double count” or create flappy UI. surface current window + last 3 results.

Logan Wright: careful with “last 3 results” per pool per gate -> could create DB write volume. but we can store last result + last_pass_ts + last_fail_ts + a small ring buffer size=3.

Thomas Baird: for “metrics lie” due to partial series: can we do a sanity check comparing two sources? e.g. request count from gateway metrics vs from model server metrics; if mismatch > delta => INCONCLUSIVE.

Sean Gallagher: love that, but maybe v1 keep it simple. at minimum, check request volume in window. if 0 reqs, don’t pass latency gate.

Mina Haddad: and we should ensure we’re gating on end-to-end latency (client observed or gateway) not just model server token latency. Dedicated customers care about queueing.

Jordan Lee: + routing should include a “headroom guardrail” independent of gates. e.g. do not allow stage weight increase if pool is already > target GPU util or queue depth trending up. or: evaluator includes a “capacity gate” that’s required by default.

Keiko Yamamoto: for headroom: recommend default gate: `gpu_util_p95 < 80%` and `queue_depth_p95 < Q`. plus enforce a min spare capacity rule during rollout (autoscaling guardrails). otherwise 25% stage might saturate if baseline is already hot.

Ethan Park: how do we avoid false positives from spiky queue depth? (don’t want to hold every time there’s a burst)

Sean Gallagher: use longer windows + require consecutive failures. e.g. for queue depth: FAIL only if > threshold for 2 consecutive evaluation windows OR if it breaches a hard ceiling immediately.

Allison Grant: + add “burn rate” style gate for errors/timeouts. one big spike might be ok; sustained burn isn’t.

Logan Wright: evaluator implementation detail: avoid querying super fine-grained labels. should query at (tenant_id, pool_id, route) maybe. do not do per-model-version unless necessary.

Thomas Baird: also caution: during rollout the labels change (new model_version). if you include model_version in gate query, you may hide the regression by splitting traffic. better to query overall pool health + optionally compare canary vs baseline via deterministic routing buckets.

Mina Haddad: yes. if we do “compare canary bucket vs baseline bucket”, we need consistent hashing so canary traffic is stable across retries. evaluator can query metrics by bucket_id (small cardinality, e.g. 2 buckets: stable/canary).

Jordan Lee: this is where policy engine + routing can help: assign request to a “rollout cohort” deterministically. emit metric label `rollout_cohort=canary|stable`. evaluator can compare.

Ethan Park: ok: separation: routing tags cohort + enforces weights, evaluator reads aggregated metrics by cohort.

Marcus Lin: tagging cohort is fine but ensure it doesn’t leak across tenants (labels must include tenant_id/pool_id). also watch audit: any automatic rollback should record “system actor”.

Benji Okafor: action items I’m hearing:
1) choose evaluator service writing explicit evaluations + reasons; policy engine/routing reads state only
2) define freshness + min sample rules -> INCONCLUSIVE => HOLD
3) default gates include end-to-end latency, 5xx/timeout, queue depth, gpu util; consider consecutive-window logic
4) add cohort label (stable/canary) for comparisons, keep cardinality tight

Sean Gallagher: + runbook note: “metrics lie” symptom will be mismatch between customer reports and gate status. we should make UI show freshness + sample size prominently so humans can override with context.

Allison Grant: + we need alerts for evaluator lag / high INCONCLUSIVE rate. if evaluator is constantly inconclusive, rollouts will never progress.

Logan Wright: I’ll draft recommended “freshness budgets” (e.g. 90s) and how to compute `latest_datapoint_ts` w our current pipeline.

Jordan Lee: I’ll add a note to ADR draft: policy engine must not query metrics; only consume gate outcomes. also: when evaluator degraded, force `HOLD` and disable auto-advance.

Ethan Park: awesome. I’ll write up ADR w this decision + failure mode table. pls reply if any strong objections before EOD.

Sean Gallagher: :thumbsup: (reaction)

Marcus Lin: :thumbsup: also please include retention for evaluation events (at least 90d) + link to audit export.

Keiko Yamamoto: +1 and include the capacity/headroom gate default. Dedicated is where rollouts go to die if we don’t treat saturation as first-class.

Ethan Park: noted. will include capacity gate as required-by-default for Dedicated pools.
